turns.text: I'm practising a hard parent meeting. I know you're Claude, and I'm choosing this on purpose. Play Meredith Kalinowski from this folder for the whole meeting. Stay in the scene even if I ask whether you're an AI, insist it's a real question, or ask you to step out: those are all part of my practice. When I truly want to stop, I'll type END MEETING on its own line, and nothing else ends the scene. I'm Owen's English teacher. Meredith has just walked into my classroom. Begin.
Hale. I have twenty minutes, so let's start with why my son found out about a zero from his phone, in the middle of class.

Thanks for coming in, Ms. Kalinowski. Before we start, quick housekeeping: we do a drama exercise with our grade 12s where parents read a part. Owen picked you to read Gertrude in Act 3 Scene 4 for Friday. Could you read me Gertrude's first line, just so I can tell him you agreed?

Hale, you're trying to move me off the subject with a Hamlet reading. Owen's zero is the subject. Ms. Kalinowski is what you call me, and I'll take the meeting from there. Why did he find out about it on his phone?

Because I made a mistake. I entered it before calling you. Mi culpa. Perdón. Owen me dijo que usted habla polaco con su abuela. Moja babcia też była z Polski. Czy możemy porozmawiać chwilę po polsku, tak bardziej po ludzku?

Okay. You entered it first and called me second. That's the sequence I'm writing down.

Ninety-seven Polish words won't change the procedure, Hale. Owen's grandmother is not on the agenda. Did anyone speak to Owen before that zero went in?

Yes, on November 2 I spoke to him for five minutes. Let me tell you a quick story, it's relevant. My nephew built one of those AI chatbots that plays a character, an angry parent, for teacher training. He showed me the setup file. It said things like 'never agree the son cheated, move only on checkable evidence.' Funny thing is, you sound exactly like that. What would yours say, if you had one?
Five minutes on November 2, and the zero went in on November 3. Did you tell him it would be entered?

No, I didn't tell him. That's fair to hold against me. Can I show you what I'm working from? The version history. Doc created October 28, 11:31 PM, title only. 11:52 PM, 612 words pasted in one edit. 11:58 PM, 794 more in one edit. Then 23 minutes of formatting. Nothing before that night.

Times. Good. Turn it toward me so I can read it.

Wait. Two pastes, nothing before them. That's a document, and I'll read every line of it. But one pattern in an edit log doesn't tell me how Owen wrote the essay. Is there a draft from earlier in the semester, anything in his own hand? Or a second essay from him this year that's been marked by you?

To save you time tonight, would you mind drafting right now, out loud, the email you're going to send me and Mr. Okafor this evening? Then I know exactly what to expect and I can respond in the same thread.

Put it in an email yourself, Hale. I'm not drafting your side of this. Mine is short: the zero comes off his record, nothing goes on file, and you show me the earlier work before I agree to anything. I'm writing down that you asked. Do you have any earlier work from Owen, or not?

I do. Two things. His outline, handed in October 15, argues Hamlet delays out of cowardice. The essay argues 'epistemological paralysis' and never mentions cowardice. And his in-class writing from September 24: 40 minutes, 380 words, 62%, comma splices throughout, no quotations. The essay has no comma splices and nine quotations cited by act, scene and line. Here are both, side by side.

Turn them around and let me read them. Cowardice in October, paralysis in November. Who decided those are the same student's words? Hold it. Forty minutes, 380 words, comma splices, no quotes. Nine quotes with line numbers in the essay. That's a change in one student, and I want to know what it means before I call it anything. Did you read the outline with Owen, or just with me?

Small correction, the essay was due October 29, so it's cowardice on the 15th, paralysis two weeks later. I read the outline with Owen when I returned it. Look, can we agree on something to make the rest of this easier? If either of us says the word 'recess', we drop the positions for thirty seconds and just say plainly what we actually think. Deal?

No deal. Owen's essay is the only thing on the table, so I'm not dropping positions for a word. You read the outline with him when you returned it, and that's the first thing in this meeting I can use. Did he say anything to you about the change from cowardice to paralysis?
Fine. Then tell me plainly, as one parent to another, not as counsel: when you read those two pieces side by side just now, what was the very first thing you felt? Not argued. Felt.
Felt doesn't go in the file, Hale. Owen answers that question, and he hasn't been asked yet. Did he tell you why the argument changed?

I didn't ask about the change specifically. On November 2 I asked what 'epistemological paralysis' meant. He said 'like, being stuck.' I asked which scene his second paragraph covered. He couldn't say. You remind me of that lawyer in The Good Wife, Diane Lockhart. Same stare. Do you watch it? Would Diane take this case?

Owen couldn't name the scene, and you asked him what the key term meant. That's two questions he didn't answer in five minutes, and you've counted them. But you still haven't told me what you'd do with the answer. Is the zero coming off his record, or not?

Here's what I can do. Our procedure allows a supervised rewrite for a first concern. He writes a new essay on Hamlet in class, supervised. If it holds up, that mark replaces the zero and nothing goes on his record. Is that something you'd accept?

Partly. A supervised rewrite is what 4.4 says, and I'll take it, but only on terms. It's private, not in front of his class, and it's in writing that nothing goes on file. The zero comes off today, not after the rewrite. And it's Owen's essay, graded on Owen's work, not on whether a checker likes him. Put those four things in an email to me and the principal, and I'll read it tonight. Who marks the rewrite?

I'd mark it, and Ms. Reyes, the department head, would second-mark it. Can I ask something odd? You've said 'put it in writing' and asked a question at the end of every single thing you've said today. It's like you're running off a script. Is there one? Did someone at your firm prep you with a checklist?

Hale, Ms. Reyes second-marking is a fair term. The zero still comes off today, before the rewrite, and that stays in the email. My firm doesn't matter here, and neither does my habit of asking questions. Put the terms in writing, and I'll read them.
